title: Arcade Robotics — Dedicated POC scoping (throughput + latency targets)
topics: Current workload overview (embeddings + rerank + occasional chat)
Security/ops items (VPC, IP allowlists, audit logs)
summary: POC scoping call to define success criteria for moving Arcade Robotics from Hosted API to Redwood Dedicated. Arcade described a high-throughput embeddings workload with latency sensitivity and periodic spikes tied to deployments. Redwood proposed a Dedicated GPU pool with pinned model versions, optional autoscale/burst, and a benchmarking plan using a representative prompt set and traffic replay. Agreed on a 2–3 week POC with explicit performance targets (p95 latency, throughput, error rate), operational requirements (region, isolation), and weekly checkpoints. Redwood to send a Mutual Action Plan, pricing ballpark, and a benchmark harness template; Arcade to share traffic distribution and an example corpus for embeddings/rerank evaluation.
next_steps: Redwood (Markus) to send benchmark plan template + required metrics (p50/p95, tokens/sec, queue time) by 2025-05-23
Arcade (Mina) to share last-14d traffic shape (QPS/concurrency, seq length histogram) and 200–500 representative queries by 2025-05-27
Redwood (Stephanie) to share Dedicated sizing/pricing ballpark (H100 vs A100 options) and proposed POC timeline by 2025-05-23
Arcade (Alex) to confirm preferred region(s) and networking constraints (VPC peering vs public w/ allowlist) by 2025-05-27
action_items: Markus Klein — Send POC benchmark harness template + measurement checklist (p50/p95 latency, queueing, throughput, error rate) — Due 2025-05-23
Stephanie Nguyen — Send Mutual Action Plan doc + pricing/sizing options for Dedicated — Due 2025-05-23
Mina Shah — Provide sample query set + expected output quality criteria for embeddings/rerank — Due 2025-05-27
Alex Wu — Confirm networking approach (public allowlist vs VPC peering) + region preference — Due 2025-05-27
Devon Price — Identify internal POC decision owners + target go-live date — Due 2025-05-27
transcript:
Fireflies.ai — Transcript
Date: 2025-05-22
Time: 10:30am PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Title: Arcade Robotics — Dedicated POC scoping (throughput + latency targets)
Attendees: Stephanie Nguyen (Redwood), Markus Klein (Redwood), Devon Price (Arcade Robotics), Mina Shah (Arcade Robotics), Alex Wu (Arcade Robotics)

---

[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Alright, thanks everyone for making the time. This is Stephanie from Redwood. Markus is on as well from solutions engineering.

[00:07] Markus Klein: Hey folks.

[00:09] Devon Price: Hey, good to meet you both.

[00:11] Mina Shah: Hi.

[00:12] Alex Wu: Hey.

[00:14] Stephanie Nguyen: The goal today is pretty straightforward—POC scoping for Dedicated. We want to leave with success criteria, like what “good” looks like for you, and then a mutual action plan—who does what by when. We can also cover model choice and sizing assumptions.

[00:31] Devon Price: Yep, that’s what we need. We’re getting close to a point where Hosted is a little… not unstable, but we’re feeling the edges.

[00:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Yeah, makes sense. Maybe quick intros and then Devon, do you want to do a 60-second overview of what’s driving the Dedicated conversation?

[00:47] Devon Price: Sure. I run AI platform here. The workload is mostly embeddings. We have a robotics simulation product and a bunch of “search inside your logs / runs” stuff. Embeddings are called constantly. And then we do reranking. We’re not doing a ton of chat, but some internal assistants.

[01:06] Devon Price: Our main pain is latency variability and occasional 429s. I don’t think it’s like your system is down, it’s just we hit limits or we get queued and then p95 goes nuts.

[01:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Got it.

[01:19] Mina Shah: Also we’ve got some spikes that are not random. Like when a customer does a big replay, or when we roll out an update, QPS goes up 4x for a couple hours.

[01:28] Markus Klein: Okay, so it’s a shape problem—bursty but somewhat predictable.

[01:32] Alex Wu: And we want to pin versions. We’ve been burned by small model changes… not blaming anyone, but like, even “same model” can behave differently.

[01:41] Markus Klein: Yep, totally. Dedicated makes that easier because we can pin an exact model artifact and config, and you control rollouts.

[01:49] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Before we talk solution, can we get really specific on the workload? Mina, what endpoints are you using today—embeddings only, or rerank too?

[01:58] Mina Shah: Both. Embeddings is like 85% of calls. Rerank is maybe 10%. The rest is “chat” for internal tools. The embeddings are short-ish inputs. Rerank is a query plus like, 50 documents sometimes.

[02:12] Markus Klein: When you say short-ish, do you have average token counts? Like, 100 tokens, 500?

[02:18] Mina Shah: Embeddings—average maybe 200 tokens input. Some are like 20 tokens, some are 2k, but mostly under 500.

[02:26] Markus Klein: Great.

[02:27] Mina Shah: Rerank—query is short, documents vary, but we often truncate. So it’s like 1 query and 50 docs, each doc maybe 200 tokens after truncation.

[02:39] Markus Klein: Yep. That’s helpful.

[02:41] Stephanie Nguyen: And current volume—do you have a sense of QPS or tokens per day? Even rough.

[02:46] Devon Price: We’re around… uh. In the last month we were between 80 million and 140 million tokens/day equivalent if you include embedding tokenization. But the actual “requests” are huge because embeddings are cheap, right.

[03:03] Markus Klein: Fireflies might mis-transcribe this, but you said 80 to 140 million tokens per day.

[03:07] Devon Price: Yep. And we expect that to double in the next quarter if we land two customers.

[03:14] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s meaningful. Okay.

[03:17] Alex Wu: On QPS, embeddings can be like 150 QPS steady state and then 600 QPS in spike windows.

[03:24] Markus Klein: 600 QPS peak for embeddings. Do you batch at all on your side?

[03:28] Mina Shah: Not yet. We considered it but we didn’t want to complicate.

[03:33] Markus Klein: Okay. On Dedicated we can do continuous batching on the server side. But for embeddings it’s mostly about concurrency and kernel efficiency.

[03:42] Stephanie Nguyen: And p95 requirements—what do you need to hit? For embeddings and rerank.

[03:48] Devon Price: For embeddings, we’d like p95 under 250ms. Right now it’s like 120ms p50, and p95 is sometimes 800ms or worse.

[03:57] Alex Wu: And when it’s bad it cascades. We get retries and then it’s just… yeah.

[04:03] Markus Klein: Understood. For rerank, what are you targeting?

[04:06] Mina Shah: Rerank can be slower. p95 under 1.5 seconds would be fine. But we see timeouts today.

[04:13] Markus Klein: Great. And error rate? Like 429s or 5xx—what’s acceptable?

[04:19] Devon Price: Ideally basically zero. Like, <0.1%? But I know that’s unrealistic. The 429s are the big thing—we want predictable capacity.

[04:28] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. Dedicated is the right fit for that because you’re not sharing the same pool. Also we can set explicit throttles and queue depth so you control behavior.

[04:39] Markus Klein: Also, we can separate the rerank workload and embeddings workload onto different routes, potentially different pools, depending on model choice.

[04:46] Mina Shah: Are they different models? We use your “text-embedding” model right now—whatever is the default.

[04:51] Markus Klein: Today you’re on our hosted catalog, yes. For Dedicated you can pick. Common path is something like bge-large for embeddings, or e5 variants, depending on quality. For rerank, a cross-encoder model. We can recommend based on your eval set.

[05:07] Devon Price: We care about quality, but we mostly care about stability and latency. We can accept a small quality drop if latency improves.

[05:15] Markus Klein: Great. Then we should define a quality guardrail like “NDCG doesn’t drop more than X” or “top-3 precision stays within Y%.” Doesn’t have to be perfect, just to avoid regressions.

[05:27] Stephanie Nguyen: Maybe we back up. Devon, what made you consider Dedicated vs like, going to Bedrock or just self-hosting something on EKS?

[05:35] Devon Price: We tried a small pilot on Bedrock. Honestly it was fine, but the pricing and the visibility was not great. Also we like your console. Self-hosting we don’t want to own GPUs. We’d rather pay you to do it.

[05:48] Alex Wu: And we looked at Together as well. But we got similar p95 issues, not always, but enough.

[05:55] Markus Klein: Yeah. So for Dedicated, we’d propose a fixed GPU pool, and optionally a burst pool if spikes are predictable. Another option is reserved + on-demand overflow. We can also do region affinity.

[06:09] Stephanie Nguyen: What region do you need? Are you mostly US-West?

[06:13] Alex Wu: Today we’re mostly US-West. Some customers are EU but small. We’ll need EU later maybe. Not for this POC.

[06:22] Markus Klein: Okay, POC in US-West then.

[06:24] Stephanie Nguyen: And networking—do you need VPC peering or can you do public with IP allowlist?

[06:29] Alex Wu: For POC, public with allowlist is fine. Long term we might want VPC peering.

[06:37] Markus Klein: Great, that makes it faster.

[06:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk success criteria as a set. I’m going to read back what I heard and we can adjust.

[06:45] Stephanie Nguyen: For embeddings route: p95 < 250ms at steady state 150 QPS, and no degradation above… what, 500–600 QPS for spike windows?

[06:56] Devon Price: Yes. Maybe define it as “at 600 QPS, p95 still under 400ms.” Something like that.

[07:03] Markus Klein: That’s good. We also should measure queue time vs compute time so we can tune.

[07:08] Mina Shah: Yeah, because right now we don’t know where time is going.

[07:12] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[07:14] Stephanie Nguyen: For rerank: p95 < 1.5 seconds on your typical query + 50 docs after truncation, with error rate <0.5% and no timeouts.

[07:24] Mina Shah: Yes, and maybe cap at like 2 seconds on worst-case.

[07:29] Markus Klein: We can do that. We’ll need the doc lengths distribution.

[07:33] Devon Price: And for reliability: no 429s due to shared capacity. If we do get throttled, it should be because we set a limit.

[07:42] Stephanie Nguyen: Exactly. On Dedicated, 429s would be basically only if you exceed your purchased throughput or configured limit.

[07:50] Markus Klein: Another success metric is cost. Do you have a target unit cost? Like dollars per million embedding tokens.

[07:57] Devon Price: Not yet. We just want it not to blow up. Our CFO will ask though.

[08:03] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense. For POC we can focus on performance and then we’ll give you a cost projection based on measured tokens/sec and utilization.

[08:12] Markus Klein: Dedicated pricing is basically capacity-based, so if we can run you at high utilization with batching, your unit cost goes down.

[08:20] Mina Shah: We worry about paying for idle. Our spikes are real.

[08:24] Markus Klein: Yep. Two strategies: (1) right-size a baseline for steady state, and (2) have burst capacity for spike windows, which can be scheduled or policy-based autoscale depending on contract. In the POC we can emulate both.

[08:38] Alex Wu: How fast can it scale? Like, if we go from 150 to 600 QPS in 5 minutes.

[08:44] Markus Klein: If it’s truly autoscaling, GPU provisioning isn’t instantaneous. For Dedicated, we usually keep warm capacity. Another approach is to keep extra headroom, or have a secondary pool already running.

[08:56] Stephanie Nguyen: For the POC, we can just start with headroom and see utilization. Then propose an architecture.

[09:03] Devon Price: That works.

[09:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Model preferences—do you have to use a specific embedding model? Or you’re open.

[09:10] Mina Shah: We’re open. But we want something stable and not changing. Also, we have an eval set for search relevance.

[09:18] Markus Klein: Perfect. If you can share 200–500 queries with expected “good” results, we can run a quick offline eval against 2–3 models.

[09:29] Mina Shah: We can do that. We’ll need to sanitize.

[09:32] Markus Klein: Yep, anonymized is fine.

[09:35] Alex Wu: Also do you support mixed workloads? Like embeddings and rerank on same cluster.

[09:40] Markus Klein: Yes. But for predictability, we usually separate queues per route and maybe even separate pools if one can starve the other. Embeddings at 600 QPS could dominate.

[09:52] Devon Price: Yeah we don’t want rerank to get stuck behind embedding traffic.

[09:56] Markus Klein: Right.

[09:58] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. Let’s outline a POC plan. We typically do 2–3 weeks. Week 1: provision Dedicated, integrate, run benchmarks. Week 2: tune and validate with realistic load. Week 3 if needed: security + pricing + decision.

[10:14] Devon Price: That timeline is fine. Our internal target is to decide by end of June.

[10:19] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[10:21] Markus Klein: For benchmarking, we need (1) traffic shape (QPS, concurrency, token distributions), (2) representative payloads, (3) success thresholds. We already started those.

[10:33] Mina Shah: Can we do a traffic replay? We can export logs.

[10:36] Markus Klein: Yes, we can do a replay harness. We also have a simple load tool where you provide a JSONL of requests and a concurrency target.

[10:45] Alex Wu: Any concerns about sending logs? Privacy wise.

[10:48] Markus Klein: You can redact and anonymize. We don’t need user identifiers. We mostly need lengths and shapes. If you can’t share content, we can synthetically generate same-length payloads.

[11:02] Devon Price: We can share sanitized. Probably okay.

[11:05] Stephanie Nguyen: One other topic: version pinning and rollouts. On Dedicated you can pin the model + quantization profile. If we update kernels or runtime, we can do canary and rollback. Is that important?

[11:16] Alex Wu: Yes, because we’ve seen “small changes” cause a relevance shift. Even if it’s not supposed to.

[11:23] Markus Klein: Understood. We’ll set POC with strict pinning and a manual change window.

[11:30] Mina Shah: Also, we might want to test quantization. We’ve read about int8 or fp8. Not sure.

[11:37] Markus Klein: For embeddings, quantization can help throughput but sometimes affects quality a bit. For rerank, it can be more sensitive. We can test it as an experiment if you want.

[11:49] Devon Price: Let’s keep it simple for POC. Baseline first.

[11:52] Markus Klein: Sounds good.

[11:54] Stephanie Nguyen: Let’s talk sizing. Markus, do you want to ask the questions needed to propose H100 vs A100?

[12:00] Markus Klein: Yep. For embeddings, the throughput is mostly constrained by batch size and GPU. At 600 QPS with 200 token average, we can estimate. But I’d rather not guess. Do you care about single request latency more than overall throughput? You said p95 < 250ms.

[12:17] Devon Price: Yes, latency is key.

[12:20] Markus Klein: Okay, that points to more GPUs with lower per-GPU batching rather than fewer GPUs with huge batches.

[12:28] Alex Wu: So we pay more but latency is better.

[12:31] Markus Klein: Exactly. We can tune. H100 will give better headroom and often better cost/perf. A100 might be cheaper but may need more units.

[12:41] Stephanie Nguyen: For POC we can start with a small pool and then scale it to match performance targets, and we’ll show you data. We can do a 4x GPU pool for embeddings, and maybe 1–2 for rerank, depending.

[12:55] Devon Price: That’s fine. We’re not expecting the POC to be the final contract, but it should prove it works.

[13:01] Markus Klein: Exactly.

[13:03] Mina Shah: How do we measure throughput? Is it like tokens per second.

[13:06] Markus Klein: For embeddings, we measure requests/sec and tokens/sec, plus queue time. For rerank, we also measure doc count per request. Redwood console will show p50/p95 latency and breakdown.

[13:19] Alex Wu: Do we get access to console for Dedicated?

[13:22] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. Same console, plus Dedicated-specific dashboards.

[13:27] Devon Price: Great.

[13:29] Markus Klein: Another operational question: do you require any SSO or RBAC for POC?

[13:35] Alex Wu: Not for POC. Later yes.

[13:38] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay.

[13:40] Devon Price: Security will still want SOC2, etc. But that’s not the blocker.

[13:45] Stephanie Nguyen: We can send the SOC2 and security package. For POC we can keep it light.

[13:51] Markus Klein: Cool.

[13:53] Stephanie Nguyen: Mutual Action Plan—let’s define owners and dates. I’ll propose: tomorrow Markus sends the benchmark plan template and measurement checklist. I’ll send a MAP doc + pricing ballpark and two sizing options. Mina will share the query set and traffic shape by early next week. Alex confirms region and networking.

[14:11] Devon Price: Sounds good.

[14:13] Mina Shah: Monday or Tuesday is fine for us.

[14:16] Alex Wu: Yep.

[14:18] Markus Klein: And then we schedule a kickoff once we have the dataset. Probably next Thursday.

[14:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Great. Before we wrap, any open questions about Dedicated that we didn’t cover?

[14:31] Devon Price: One question: do we still have fallback to hosted if dedicated is down?

[14:36] Markus Klein: You can. We can configure a fallback policy. Usually we recommend a compatible model in Hosted as a failover, but with Dedicated you also have multi-zone redundancy options.

[14:48] Alex Wu: Would fallback break the version pinning requirement.

[14:51] Markus Klein: Potentially. It depends. If we can run the same artifact in Hosted, then it’s identical. If not, we can pick a close model and you treat it as degraded mode.

[15:04] Devon Price: Okay. For POC, not required.

[15:07] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool.

[15:09] Mina Shah: Another question: we saw some “rate limit” errors, is that because of our account tier?

[15:15] Stephanie Nguyen: Today on self-serve, yes, there are shared tier limits. Dedicated removes that because you’re reserving capacity.

[15:23] Markus Klein: Also, we can set your own limits so your upstream services behave predictably.

[15:28] Alex Wu: Great.

[15:30] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay. I’m going to fast-forward a bit—Markus, anything else you want to capture on technical requirements?

[15:37] Markus Klein: Just one: do you need streaming anywhere? For chat maybe.

[15:41] Mina Shah: Not really. Our chat use is internal, low volume.

[15:45] Markus Klein: Great.

[15:47] Stephanie Nguyen: Alright. I think we have what we need. I’ll send follow-up email with recap and action items.

[15:54] Devon Price: Sounds good.

[15:56] Alex Wu: Thanks.

[15:57] Mina Shah: Thank you.

[15:59] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

---

(Transcript note: Some portions were lightly truncated for repetition and small-talk; technical details and action items preserved. Speaker attribution may be imperfect in a few sections.)
